```{r}
#| label: setup
#| eval: false
library(DeCovarT)
```

The bivariate toy and the covariance-driven scenario use a population
reference: every cell type is one purified Gaussian profile, and the bulk
is their convolution. This scenario uses a **single-cell** reference:
the bulk is the sum of $n_i$ cells, each drawn from the law of its type,
and DeCovarT fits the single-cell model with its two scales profiled out
([single-cell model](theory-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-profile-newton)).
The $J=4$ cell types form two lineages, types 1–2 and types 3–4, so
every type has a close sibling and a distant cousin. Construction,
benchmark and plot books live in one script,
`scripts/fig05_single_cell_hierarchical.R` (seed `20261024`).

# Generative model {#sec-sc-generative}

The generator is the single-cell model itself
([cell size in the covariance](theory-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-cell-size-covariance)).
For bulk $i$,

$$
\boldsymbol m_{\cdot i}\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n_i,\boldsymbol p),
\qquad
\boldsymbol T_{ji}\sim\mathcal N_G\bigl(m_{ji}S_j\boldsymbol\theta_{\cdot j},\;
m_{ji}S_j^{2}\boldsymbol\Sigma^{\theta}_j\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol y_{\cdot i}=a\sum_j\boldsymbol T_{ji},
$$ {#eq-fig05-generator}

where $\boldsymbol\theta_{\cdot j}$ is the expression profile of a cell
of unit size, $S_j$ the cell size of type $j$ and $a$ the platform
scale. The estimand is the **realised** cell fraction
$\boldsymbol m_{\cdot i}/n_i$, not $\boldsymbol p$
(`simulate_bulk_from_cells()` returns it as `p_realised`).

A cell $S_j$ times larger is $S_j$ times larger in every gene, so the
size multiplies the mean by $S_j$ and the covariance by $S_j^{2}$
(`rescale_single_cell_moments()`). Two consequences:

- the overlap between two types of equal size does not depend on that
  size, so cell size only moves the lineages apart and reweights the
  bulk;
- in transcript units the covariance of a cell is $S_j\boldsymbol\Sigma^{\theta}_j$,
  which is the form of the `transcript_raw` reference.

DeCovarT is fitted with the `cellular_raw` reference: cell fractions,
known cell sizes and raw covariances.

## Mean signature

One mean signature per gene count $G\in\{20,200\}$ is built by
`generate_mean_signature_matrix(target_gram = R, nonnegative = TRUE)`
([mean signature construction](theory-synthetic-scenarios-mean-covariance.html#sec-lr-block-mu)),
with mean scale $10$ and the target Gram

$$
R=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0.8 & 0.3 & 0.3\\
0.8 & 1 & 0.3 & 0.3\\
0.3 & 0.3 & 1 & 0.8\\
0.3 & 0.3 & 0.8 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-fig05-gram}

The cosine between lineages is $0.3$, not $0.1$. With non-negative
means, the expression of a gene in the other lineage is then about
$13\%$ of its main level; at a cosine of $0.1$ it would be about $4\%$,
close to disjoint marker blocks, and the scenario would reduce to
marker-gene deconvolution. Every gene is expressed in all four types.

## Lineage networks

Each lineage has one skeleton, shared exactly by its two siblings:

| Type | Lineage | Skeleton |
|:-----|:--------|:---------|
| celltype_1 | 1 | stochastic block model, three blocks of equal size |
| celltype_2 | 1 | the same skeleton as celltype_1 |
| celltype_3 | 2 | scale-free (Barabási–Albert, `power = 1`) |
| celltype_4 | 2 | the same skeleton as celltype_3 |

: Graph of each cell type. {#tbl-fig05-graphs}

The blocks are contiguous in gene order (`block_sizes` of
`generate_random_network_skeleton()`), with $p_{\mathrm{within}}=0.25$ and
$p_{\mathrm{between}}=0.01$. Signed weights are drawn once per lineage by
`assign_iid_signed_weights()` (half inhibitory, magnitude $0.3$); each
sibling then flips the sign of a random $5\%$ of the edges, so the two
siblings differ only by their edge weights. With independent signs the
sibling covariances differ so much at $G=200$ that a sibling overlap of
$0.08$ cannot be reached (at most $0.013$; $0.030$ with $20\%$ flips).
Precisions are completed by `build_normalised_precision()` with a fixed
spectral shift of $0.2$
([GGM networks](theory-synthetic-scenarios-mean-covariance.html#sec-ggm-networks)).

## Sibling overlap

One global covariance scale per gene count and overlap target is chosen
by `scale_covariances_to_overlap(pairs = rbind(c(1, 2), c(3, 4)))`, so
that the **mean overlap of the two sibling pairs** is $0.01$ or $0.08$ at
the balanced composition. Calibrating on all six pairs would let the
four nearly separated between-lineage pairs dilute the target. The
scale is calibrated once on equal cell sizes and reused for unequal
sizes, since the sibling overlap does not depend on a common size. In
the dry run the realised mean of the two sibling pairs is $0.009$ to
$0.081$. The two pairs differ (from $0.0005$ to $0.149$), because the
block model and the scale-free graph give the two lineages different
covariances. The overlaps are identical for equal and unequal sizes, and
between-lineage overlaps stay at or below $0.001$ (Monte Carlo
estimates, $10^4$ draws per type).

## Factorial design

| Factor | Levels |
|:-------|:-------|
| Composition $\boldsymbol p$ | balanced $(1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4)$; unbalanced within each lineage $(0.4,0.1,0.4,0.1)$ |
| Sibling overlap | $0.01$; $0.08$ |
| Cells per bulk $n_i$ | $10^{3}$; $10^{5}$ |
| Cell sizes $\boldsymbol S$ | $(1,1,1,1)$; $(1,1,5,5)$ |
| Genes $G$ | $20$; $200$ |
| Platform scale $a$ | $1$; $5$ |
| **Crossed scenarios** | $2^{6}=\mathbf{64}$ |

: Single-cell factorial (64 scenarios). {#tbl-fig05-factorial}

- **Cells per bulk.** With $n_i\ge10^{3}$ the rarest type counts about
  $100$ cells, so the multinomial draw does not leave a type empty.
- **Genes.** The maximum-likelihood variance scale $\hat\phi$ is biased
  down by about $(G-J)/G$, that is $0.8$ at $G=20$ and $0.98$ at $G=200$;
  the REML calibration corrects it
  ([REML](theory-single-cell-inference.html#sec-sc-reml)).
- **Platform scale.** Rescaling the bulk by $a$ rescales $\hat c$ by $a$
  and $\hat\phi$ by $a^{2}$, leaves $\hat{\boldsymbol p}$ unchanged, and
  shifts the profile log-likelihood by $-G\log a$
  ([scale equivariance](theory-single-cell-inference.html#sec-sc-setting)),
  so the estimates of $\boldsymbol p$ should agree between $a=1$ and
  $a=5$, which the crossed $a=1$ half checks numerically. It also tests
  RNA-Sieve, whose mean and variance share one scale.

Scenario identifiers read
`S{row}_{Ba|Un}_{O1|O8}_n{1e3|1e5}_{Se|Sl}_G{20|200}_a{1|5}`, for
example `S1_Ba_O1_n1e3_Se_G20_a1`.

```{r}
#| label: design
# The design takes about a minute (overlap calibration by Sobol Monte
# Carlo for each gene count and target).
benchmark <- readRDS("output/fig05/fig05_benchmark.rds")
benchmark$config |>
  dplyr::select(
    ID, proportions, overlap_target, sibling_overlap, n_cells,
    cell_size_label, n_genes, platform_scale
  )
```

# Inference {#sec-sc-inference-benchmark}

Every method is scored on the same simulated bulks, with all genes (no
feature selection).

| Method | Function or code | Input | Intervals |
|:-------|:-----------------|:------|:----------|
| `lsei` | `deconvolute_ratios_deconrnaseq()` | true means | none |
| NNLS | `deconvolute_ratios_nnls()` | true means | none |
| RLM | `deconvolute_ratios_rlm()` | true means | none |
| CIBERSORT | `deconvolute_ratios_cibersort()` | true means | none |
| Newton–Raphson | `deconvolute_single_cell(optimiser = "newton")` | true moments, known sizes | Wald, ILR, ILR-REML, profile, profile-REML, bootstrap, oracle |
| L-BFGS-B | `deconvolute_single_cell(optimiser = "lbfgsb")` | true moments, known sizes | Wald, ILR, ILR-REML, profile, profile-REML, bootstrap |
| Firth | `fit_firth_single_cell()` | true moments, known sizes | Wald, Wald-REML, ILR, ILR-REML |
| MEAD | `MEAD::MEAD()` (GitHub, commit `d66fa10`) | reference panel, cohort of $N$ bulks | native sandwich interval |
| RNA-Sieve | `rnasieve` 0.1.4 (Python) | reference panel, cohort of $N$ bulks | released, Fisher and Godambe |
| ReDeconv | `redeconv` 1.2.1 (Python) | true means and standard deviations | none |

: Methods of the single-cell benchmark. {#tbl-fig05-methods}

- **`lsei` and NNLS.** The scale $c=a\,n_i$ of a single-cell bulk is
  unknown, so `lsei`, which fixes it at one, is misspecified here. NNLS
  followed by renormalisation is the same least squares with a free scale
  ($\boldsymbol\beta=c\boldsymbol p$); it is also the starting point of
  DeCovarT and RNA-Sieve. RLM is the robust linear model of Monaco et al.,
  renormalised.
- **DeCovarT.** Newton–Raphson and L-BFGS-B maximise the same profile
  log-likelihood; L-BFGS-B works on the closure chart
  $\boldsymbol p=\boldsymbol w/\mathbf1^{\top}\boldsymbol w$, $\boldsymbol w\ge0$
  ([L-BFGS-B](theory-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-profile-lbfgsb)).
  Bootstraps refit with the optimiser of the estimate.
- **Second-generation methods** follow the protocol of the
  [covariance-driven scenario](fig03-covariance-driven.html#sec-hybrid-methods).
  MEAD and RNA-Sieve read a reference panel of $R$ individuals and $20$
  cells per type and individual, drawn by `simulate_reference_replicates()`
  with its own seed, independent of the bulks.
  - MEAD rescales every reference cell to a unit total, so its
    proportions are transcript fractions
    $q_j=p_jS_j/\sum_kp_kS_k$; with $\boldsymbol S=(1,1,5,5)$ they differ
    from the cell fractions. Its intervals are scored against both.
  - RNA-Sieve's released interval code returns $[0,1]$ when its averaged
    Hessian is ill-conditioned (version 0.1.4, `stats.py`, lines 224 and
    234). The runner also returns the two intervals of the paper,
    recomputed on all genes: Fisher, $\boldsymbol B^{-1}/G$, and Godambe,
    $\boldsymbol H^{-1}\boldsymbol B\boldsymbol H^{-\top}/G$, with
    $\alpha_K=1-\sum_{k<K}\alpha_k$. In the dry run ($N=5$), averaged
    over the 132 scenario and cell-type pairs, the released interval has
    mean width $0.91$ (coverage $1$), the Godambe interval $0.36$
    (coverage $0.97$) and the Fisher interval $0.002$ (coverage $0.02$).
    The per-gene scores vary far more than the Hessian predicts, since
    RNA-Sieve's model is not the generator here, so only the sandwich
    is calibrated.
  - DECALS has no public implementation and is not run.

## Interval constructions {#sec-fig05-intervals}

The menu is that of the
[single-cell inference article](theory-single-cell-inference.html#sec-sc-intervals):

| Interval | Construction |
|:---------|:-------------|
| `wald` | delta method on $\boldsymbol p$ from the Schur-complement information |
| `ilr` | Wald in ILR coordinates mapped back to the simplex |
| `profile` | likelihood-ratio inversion with $c$ and $\phi$ profiled out |
| `*_reml` | REML calibration with $\nu=G-J$: Student quantiles and $\hat\phi$ rescaled by $G/\nu$ |
| `bootstrap` | percentile interval of a parametric bootstrap refitted by the same optimiser |
| `oracle` | $\hat p_j$ plus or minus the Wald half-width at the true composition |

: Single-cell interval menu. {#tbl-fig05-menu}

Wald, ILR and bootstrap intervals also cover the two scales,
$c=a\,n_i$ and $\phi=a^{2}n_i$ (rows `mean_scale` and `variance_scale`
of the interval table), and the platform scale $a=\phi/c$ and the cell
count $n=c^{2}/\phi$ (rows `platform_scale_a` and `cell_count_n`),
against their true values. The intervals of $a$ and $n$ are formed on the
log scale, so both bounds are positive; $\hat n$ is a number of cells
here only because $a$ is known to the generator. Coverage is reported
with a Wilson Monte Carlo interval [@morrisUsingSimulationStudies2019].

## Run size

| Variable | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `DECOVART_N_REPLICATES` | Monte Carlo bulks per scenario, $N$ | 100 |
| `DECOVART_N_BOOT` | parametric-bootstrap refits per bulk, $B$ | 200 |
| `DECOVART_N_REFERENCE` | individuals of the reference panel, $R$ | $N$ |
| `DECOVART_CORES` | workers of the per-sample loop | 1 |
| `DECOVART_POSTPROCESS_ONLY` | `1` redraws the figures from the saved benchmark | 0 |

: Run-size variables of `scripts/fig05_single_cell_hierarchical.R`. {#tbl-fig05-run-size}

Parallel workers load the **installed** DeCovarT, so run
`devtools::install()` before setting `DECOVART_CORES` above 1.

```{r}
#| label: inference
# Dry run:
#   DECOVART_N_REPLICATES=5 DECOVART_N_BOOT=5 \
#     Rscript scripts/fig05_single_cell_hierarchical.R
benchmark <- readRDS("output/fig05/fig05_benchmark.rds")
# Coverage of the composition and of the two scales.
dplyr::select(
  benchmark$intervals,
  ID, algorithm, ci_method, parameter, coverage, coverage_lower,
  coverage_upper, mean_width
)
```

# Visualisations {#sec-fig05-viz}

`output/fig05/fig05_benchmark.rds` holds the run settings, the design,
the true moments (`theta_true`) and every metric table;
`output/fig05/fig05_plot_data.rds` holds, for each figure file stem, the
data handed to its plot function.

```{r}
#| label: redraw
source("scripts/visualisation/load_visualisation.R")
plot_data <- readRDS("output/fig05/fig05_plot_data.rds")
names(plot_data)
render_figure_from_data("ci_width_forest", plot_data, "output/fig05")
```

The books follow those of the
[covariance-driven scenario](fig03-covariance-driven.html#sec-hybrid-viz),
with these changes:

- pages follow @fig-single-cell-hierarchy: $G$, then $n_i$, the
  composition and the sibling overlap; each page is a $2\times2$ panel
  with the platform scale in rows and the cell sizes in columns;
- log-likelihood surfaces are drawn on the two **within-lineage**
  balances, $1\mid2$ and $3\mid4$, with the between-lineage balance held
  at its true value, each panel zoomed on its own peak;
- CIBERSORT is left out of the RMSE and Aitchison heatmaps and of the
  RMSE dot book, where its large error squeezed the shared colour scale;
- the scenario descriptors add $n_i$, $G$ and the cell-size ratio;
- the forests add the REML-calibrated ILR and profile intervals, and
  `performance_visualisations/ci_width_forest_nuisance.pdf` gives the
  intervals of $c$, $\phi$, $a$ and $n$ on $\log_{10}$ axes;
- `performance_visualisations/nuisance_scale_ratio.pdf` shows
  $\hat c/c$ and $\hat\phi/\phi$ against the number of genes and of
  cells, with the REML-rescaled $\hat\phi\,G/(G-J)$.

# Caveats {#sec-fig05-caveats}

- **Gaussian cells.** A sum of Gaussian cells is exactly Gaussian at
  any $n_i$, so the central-limit argument behind the bulk model is not
  itself tested; a count layer would be needed for that.
- **Negative values.** Between $21\%$ and $29\%$ of the simulated
  single-cell values are negative. The reference panels of MEAD and
  RNA-Sieve receive them as such.
- **Per-cell overlap and bulk precision.** The sibling overlap describes
  the reference; the precision of a bulk also grows with $n_i$, which the
  expected Wald standard error reported with each scenario captures.
